items.title: Star performers always come back down — not because of psychology
items.claim: A rookie has a breakout season. The next year, his performance drops. Headlines say 'sophomore slump' and 'pressure of expectations'. A statistician would have predicted the drop without ever watching a game.

options.text: Extreme observations have a luck component; the next observation typically regresses toward the underlying mean. The 'rookie season' was partially luck; the next season's mean performance reflects underlying skill, with less luck

items.reveal_title: Galton, sons of tall fathers, and luck
items.reveal:
Francis Galton (1886) measured heights of fathers and sons. He noticed: tall fathers tend to have shorter sons, and short fathers tend to have taller sons. Not because fathers' height 'reverts' to a population mean, but because extreme parental heights are partly random (chance of which alleles were inherited from grandparents).

Galton called this 'regression to mediocrity', later 'regression to the mean'. The term 'regression analysis' for fitting lines to data descends from this observation.

General principle: if a measurement combines skill (or any persistent factor) and chance, extreme measurements come from combinations of GOOD skill AND GOOD luck. Replicate the measurement, and on average the luck component will be average — so the second measurement regresses toward the underlying skill mean.

Applications:
- Sports: 'sophomore slump' is regression, not psychology.
- Medicine: patients with extreme symptoms tend to improve at the next visit (regression to a less-extreme baseline). Many treatments look effective in uncontrolled trials simply because of regression.
- Education: 'praise reduces performance, criticism improves it' (Kahneman's famous Israeli pilot training observation) — actually regression after extreme performances followed by interventions.
- Finance: top-performing fund managers tend to revert toward average; investors who chase last year's winners underperform.

Correct analysis requires CONTROL groups or careful baseline modelling. Without them, regression masquerades as 'real' effects.
items.why: Performance fluctuations get psychological explanations they don't need. The math of extreme values guarantees that record-breakers tend to come back down. Understanding regression to the mean dissolves many spurious 'effects'.

items.title: Compounding interest infinitely fast gives the same answer as compounding once
items.claim: Invest 1 dollar at 100 percent annual interest. Compounded once a year: 2 dollars. Twice: 2.25. Monthly: 2.61. Continuously: 2.71828... — the constant e. Not infinity, not 2 — a specific irrational number.
items.prompt: Why does compounding infinitely often give a finite limit?

options.text: (1 + 1/n) to the power n is bounded above by 3 for all n, and increases monotonically; its limit as n approaches infinity is e, a fundamental constant of growth
Each compounding adds tiny amounts that cancel each other
Math caps results at e by definition

items.reveal:
Jacob Bernoulli, investigating compound interest, asked what happens as compounding frequency goes to infinity. He calculated (1 + 1/n) to the power n for ever-larger n and found the values approached a specific number between 2.71 and 2.72.

The number is e — base of the natural logarithm. It shows up everywhere: continuous growth (e to the rt), the normal distribution (Gauss), Euler's identity (e to the i pi equals minus 1), derangements in combinatorics, and the most-common-digit problem (Benford's law).

e can be characterised many ways:
- Limit of (1 + 1/n) to the power n.
- Infinite sum 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! + ...
- Unique number whose exponential function equals its own derivative.

Like pi, e is transcendental — no polynomial with rational coefficients has e as a root.
items.why: Compounding 'more often' sounds like it should produce ever-larger returns. The limit is finite because each compounding period adds proportionally less.

items.title: Half the world's billionaires got there partly by luck
items.claim: Repeated coin flips produce some very lucky streaks. The proportion of 'successful' (still in business, in market, alive) entities at the top of a population sample is dominated by selection effects — the unsuccessful disappear from view, leaving the survivors looking exceptional.

options.text: Survivorship bias: we only see the successes, and infer skill from outcomes; randomness alone would have produced some 'winners' from a starting pool, but we don't see the matching losers

items.reveal_title: Survivorship bias and the law of large pools
items.reveal:
If 10,000 hedge fund managers each pick stocks randomly for 10 years, about (1/1024) * 10,000 ≈ 10 will have called the market right 10 years running (by pure luck). These 10 will be on the cover of business magazines, will publish books on their 'secrets', and will attract investor billions.

The other 9,990 are out of business and forgotten.

Mochon and Norton (2011, 2012) replicated this in the lab: random stock-picking among 'subjects' produced 'expert' track records statistically indistinguishable from actual hedge funds. Selection of survivors creates the illusion of skill.

Real-world cases:
- WWII US bombers: aircraft returning from missions had bullet holes in wings and fuselage, not engines or cockpits. The Air Force initially considered reinforcing where the holes were — until Abraham Wald pointed out: planes hit in the engine or cockpit don't return. Reinforce the unhit areas.
- Famous 'success stories' (Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, J.K. Rowling) tell entrepreneurs what to do — but tens of thousands who tried the same things failed.
- Stock market: survivor-bias-corrected returns are ~1-2% per year lower than uncorrected indices, because failed stocks drop out.

The correct statistical question is not 'what did successful X do?' but 'what's the base rate of success among everyone who tried that?'.
items.why: Success seems instructive. Survivorship bias means we systematically learn from outliers and ignore the (invisible) ordinary cases. The math of selection effects is more important than the stories of any individual.
